meta.title: Imperium — the Roman economy, c. 200 AD
meta.notes: Populations are scholarly best guesses (Frier, Hanson, Wilson, Scheidel) for the Severan empire before the 3rd-century crisis. Prices are from Diocletian's Price Edict (301 AD) in denarii communes (d.c.), converted to per-kg. Freight costs come from the ORBIS network model (Scheidel/Meeks, Stanford), whose expense unit is d.c. per kg of grain — the same unit, so freight adds directly to prices. Consumption rates and mine/press outputs are stylised.

italia.name: Italia
italia.blurb: The imperial core: wine, oil, wool, Arretine ware, Luna marble — but a net grain importer. Rome alone eats a quarter-million tonnes a year.

sicilia.name: Sicilia
sicilia.blurb: Rome's first province and first breadbasket — still shipping wheat after four centuries.

sardinia_corsica.name: Sardinia et Corsica
sardinia_corsica.blurb: Grain, granite and malaria; one of the annona's quiet workhorses.

africa.name: Africa Proconsularis & Numidia
africa.blurb: The empire's largest grain supplier by the 2nd century — two-thirds of Rome's annona — plus olive oil, African Red Slip ware and wild beasts for the arena.

cyrenaica.name: Cyrenaica
cyrenaica.blurb: Grain and horses; the silphium that made it rich is already extinct.

mauretania.name: Mauretania
mauretania.blurb: Purple dye works, citrus wood, and the western limit of the olive belt.

aegyptus.name: Aegyptus
aegyptus.blurb: The Nile: the most productive farmland in the ancient world. Feeds Alexandria, ships ~20M modii to Rome, and monopolises papyrus and the Red Sea trade.

baetica.name: Baetica
baetica.blurb: Olive oil on an industrial scale — Monte Testaccio in Rome is 53 million of its amphorae — plus garum and Sierra Morena silver.

lusitania.name: Lusitania
lusitania.blurb: Garum, horses, and gold washing down from the north.

tarraconensis.name: Hispania Tarraconensis
tarraconensis.blurb: Silver at Carthago Nova, Las Médulas gold, Layetanian wine, Bilbilis steel.

narbonensis.name: Gallia Narbonensis
narbonensis.blurb: 'More Italy than a province' — mass-market wine and the La Graufesenque potteries.

aquitania.name: Aquitania
aquitania.blurb: Grain and wine down the Garonne through Burdigala.

lugdunensis.name: Gallia Lugdunensis
lugdunensis.blurb: Lugdunum: mint, customs hub, and crossroads of the Gallic river trade.

belgica.name: Gallia Belgica
belgica.blurb: Wool country — the hooded Belgic cloak is worn across the empire.

germania_inferior.name: Germania Inferior
germania_inferior.blurb: Legionary frontier; the army eats most of what the land yields.

germania_superior.name: Germania Superior
germania_superior.blurb: Rhine garrisons, terra sigillata kilns, and the Moselle vineyards beginning.

britannia.name: Britannia
britannia.blurb: Cornish tin, lead-silver, wool cloaks, and grain that will one day feed the Rhine army.

raetia.name: Raetia
raetia.blurb: Alpine passes; more customs post than farm.

noricum.name: Noricum
noricum.blurb: Ferrum Noricum — the finest steel in the empire.

pannonia.name: Pannonia
pannonia.blurb: The Danube army's marchland; the Amber Road crosses at Carnuntum.

dalmatia.name: Dalmatia
dalmatia.blurb: Timber, mines in the interior, and the great port of Salona.

moesia.name: Moesia
moesia.blurb: Lower Danube grain plains behind a legionary screen.

dacia.name: Dacia
dacia.blurb: Trajan's conquest: the Alburnus Maior gold mines are the imperial treasury's prize.

thracia.name: Thracia
thracia.blurb: Wheat, horses and hardy soldiers; Byzantium tolls the Pontic grain ships.

macedonia.name: Macedonia & Epirus
macedonia.blurb: The Via Egnatia's spine; timber and mines that once paid for Alexander.

achaea.name: Achaea
achaea.blurb: Old Greece: oil, Pentelic marble and prestige — but it has imported grain since Pericles.

creta.name: Creta
creta.blurb: Wine, honey and medicinal herbs on the Egypt run.

cyprus.name: Cyprus
cyprus.blurb: The island that named copper (aes Cyprium).

asia.name: Asia
asia.blurb: The richest, most urbanised province: wool at Laodicea, marble at Proconnesus, and a dozen great cities.

bithynia_pontus.name: Bithynia et Pontus
bithynia_pontus.blurb: Timber, Sinopean garum and the Bosporus tolls.

galatia.name: Galatia
galatia.blurb: Anatolian wool and wheat on the great east road.

cappadocia.name: Cappadocia
cappadocia.blurb: Imperial horse studs and the Euphrates frontier.

cilicia.name: Cilicia
cilicia.blurb: A fertile plain between Taurus timber and the sea; linen at Tarsus.

lycia_pamphylia.name: Lycia et Pamphylia
lycia_pamphylia.blurb: Harbours, cedar and the corn ships' lee shore.

syria.name: Syria & Phoenice
syria.blurb: Antioch's hinterland: oil and wine from the limestone hills, Tyrian purple, Sidonian glass, and the silk road's western gate at Palmyra.

palaestina.name: Syria Palaestina
palaestina.blurb: Olives, Gazan wine, Scythopolis linen, Jericho balsam.

arabia.name: Arabia Petraea
arabia.blurb: The incense caravans' toll road, annexed from the Nabataeans in 106.

mesopotamia.name: Mesopotamia & Osrhoene
mesopotamia.blurb: Severus' new frontier beyond the Euphrates, astride the Persian trade.

bosporanum.name: Bosporan Kingdom (client)
bosporanum.blurb: Crimean wheat has fed the Aegean since Athens' golden age; a client kingdom outside the frontier.

cities.note: A million mouths. The annona ships ~250,000 t of grain a year; Monte Testaccio grows by 500,000 oil amphorae a decade.
Rome's harbour: Claudius' and Trajan's basins, the warehouses of the annona.
The old Alexandrian grain terminus, still the Campanian luxury port.
Bronze workshops and the Falernian vineyards nearby.
Famous fine wool, dyed with local murex.
Gateway to Greece and the East.
Po valley wool; Strabo ranked its cloth trade first in Italy.
Amber terminus, Istrian oil, glass, and the Alpine timber trade.
Home of the Adriatic fleet.
The marble port: Carrara white ships from here.
Arretine sigillata — the red tableware that taught Gaul.
Home of the western fleet.
Still the island's great port and grain gateway.
Second city of the West; the African annona fleet sails from here.
Olive oil port of the Sahel.
Ships Numidian giallo antico marble.
Cirta's grain port.
Camp of Legio III Augusta — the only legion in Africa.
Timgad: a veterans' colony on a perfect grid.
Septimius Severus' home town, gorging on imperial favour; olive oil and Saharan trade.
Modern Tripoli.
Cyrene's harbour.
Juba II's old capital.
Second city of the world: the Nile grain funnel, papyrus monopoly, glassworks, linen, and the Red Sea's Indian cargoes.
The city of the rubbish dumps that preserved half our papyri.
Upper Egypt; tourists already visit the Colossi.
Egypt's eastern door.
Where the Nile meets the desert roads to Myos Hormos and Berenice — every pepper sack passes here.
Aswan: granite quarries and the Nubian frontier.
Capital of Baetica; Sierra Morena silver and oil estates.
Atlantic tuna, the best garum, and shipowners rich enough to scandalise Rome.
River port of the oil country: the Baetis barges load here.
Birthplace of Trajan and Hadrian.
Lisbon: Atlantic garum works.
Provincial capital; Layetanian wine country.
The silver mines that once paid Hannibal's armies, plus esparto and garum.
Administers the Las Médulas gold workings.
León: the last legion in Spain.
First Roman colony in Gaul; wine and sigillata export hub.
Where the Rhône barges meet the sea ships.
The old Greek port, still trading after six centuries.
Garonne entrepôt; Bordeaux's first vineyards are planted.
Capital of the Three Gauls: imperial mint, customs station, wine and sigillata depot.
Autun: schools and aqueducts in Aeduan country.
A modest river town; the boatmen's guild is its proudest monument.
Rouen: the Seine's outlet toward Britain.
Orléans: the Loire portage.
Trier: wool country, and Moselle wine soon.
Reims.
Amiens: heart of the Belgic cloak trade.
Metz.
Cologne: glassworks and the Rhine fleet.
Xanten.
Bonn: legionary base.
Mainz: two legions watch the Rhine.
Strasbourg.
Besançon.
The island's emporium: grain, wool cloaks, lead and tin outbound.
York: Severus died here in 211.
Colchester: the first colonia.
St Albans.
Lincoln.
Gloucester.
Chester: legionary fortress.
Bath: the sacred spring.
Exeter: outlet of the Cornish tin streams.
Augsburg.
Regensburg.
Market of the Noric iron district.
Salzburg: the salt town.
Legionary capital where the Amber Road meets the Danube.
Budapest: legion and thermae.
Rising star; a future imperial capital.
River hub and, later, a great mint.
Vienna: Marcus Aurelius died in camp here.
Diocletian will retire to grow cabbages next door.
Zadar.
Belgrade: Legio IV Flavia.
Capital of Moesia Superior.
Niš: Constantine will be born here in 272.
Legio I Italica on the Danube bank.
Ovid's grim exile, now a thriving grain port.
Varna.
Colonia Ulpia Traiana: the conquest's showpiece.
Legion base serving the Alburnus Maior gold district.
Legio V Macedonica.
At Trajan's great Danube bridge.
The northern gate of Dacia.
Thracian grain outlet on the Propontis.
Plovdiv: chief city of inland Thrace.
Edirne.
Still Byzantium — a prosperous toll town on the Bosporus, 130 years before Constantine makes it the centre of the world.
Sofia.
The Via Egnatia's great port.
Alexander's birthplace, long past its glory.
Durrës: western end of the Via Egnatia.
Augustus' victory city for Actium.
Corfu.
The university of the empire; Attic oil and Pentelic marble, but the grain ships have called since Pericles.
Refounded by Caesar; the diolkos portage and two seas' trade.
Thessalian horses and wheat.
Laconian murex and rose marble.
The oracle still speaks, mostly to tourists.
Port for Cretan wine; Gortyn, the capital, lies inland off the network.
Copper ingots stamped for export.
Aphrodite's sanctuary and the provincial capital.
First city of Asia: the Artemision, the harbour works, the banking houses.
Izmir: rival of Ephesus, port of the Hermus valley.
The Attalid citadel: parchment's namesake, Galen's hometown, the Asclepieion.
Old Lydia: gold-bearing Pactolus, wool works.
Wool and the four harbours, slowly silting.
Raven-black wool famous enough for the Apocalypse to mock its wealth.
Bodrum: the Mausoleum still stands.
Propontis port; ships Proconnesian marble.
Lesbos: wine terraces above a famous harbour.
The premium wine island since Homer.
The old maritime republic: its sea law still governs Mediterranean shipping.
Silk-gauze weaving and the Asclepieion.
Troy: the empire's most profitable ruin.
Bithynia's capital; a future imperial seat.
Iznik: Nicomedia's jealous rival.
'City of the blind', facing Byzantium.
Pontic garum, ship timber, and the red earth called sinopia.
Samsun.
Ankara: the Res Gestae is carved on its temple wall.
Konya.
Kayseri, under Mount Argaeus; the imperial horse studs.
Legio XII Fulminata on the Euphrates.
Sivas.
Temple city of Ma.
Legio XV Apollinaris.
Trebizond: the eastern fleet's Black Sea base.
Paul's hometown: linen works and the Cilician Gates.
Antalya.
Once the pirates' slave market, now respectable.
The Alexandrian grain ships shelter here — Paul changed ships at Myra.
Lycia's harbour and granary.

Its Augustan census counted 117,000 citizens; horse studs of the Seleucids.
Antioch's deep-water port.
Latakia: wine and oil port of the limestone massif.
Homs: the black stone of Elagabal; the empresses' family seat.
Hama.
Beirut: Roman law schools and Phoenician glass.
The purple city: murex vats stain the shore; its dye is worth more than gold.
Oasis market where the desert roads gather.
Tadmor: the caravan republic that walks silk across the desert from the Euphrates.
The colossal temples of Jupiter Heliopolitanus.
'The Crossing': where the Euphrates trade enters Syria.
Lucian's hometown; Legio XVI.
Herod's harbour, the provincial capital.
Aelia Capitolina since Hadrian; Jews barred from entry.
Onions (scallions!) and wine.
Incense road terminus and sweet-wine exporter.
Jaffa.
Beth Shean: the linen town.
Acre.
'Athens of the East' — philosophers and hot springs.
Legio III Cyrenaica; the Hauran grain plain.
The rose-red caravan city, tolling the frankincense road.
Amman.
Aqaba: the Red Sea's back door.
Urfa: Syriac culture's capital, lately annexed.
The designated customs post for all Persian trade.
Harran: moon-god temple; Crassus' disaster.
Dura-Europos: garrison town on the Euphrates trade lane.
Kerch: the Bosporan kings ship Scythian wheat as their ancestors did for Athens.

grain.name: Grain
grain.edictNote: wheat, 100 d.c. per castrensis modius (~10 kg); barley 60
grain.blurb: The economy's foundation: 250 kg per person per year. Cities eat their hinterland first, then buy from the great surplus regions — and freight can double the price.

olive_oil.name: Olive oil
olive_oil.blurb: Food, soap, lamp fuel and medicine. Baetica ships it to Rome on such a scale that the empties form a mountain — Monte Testaccio.

wine.name: Wine
wine.edictNote: vin ordinaire 8 d.c. per sextarius; Falernian 30
wine.blurb: Mass-market Gallic and Spanish vintages move in barrels and amphorae; Falernian and Chian fetch four times the price.

garum.name: Garum
garum.blurb: Fermented fish sauce — the ketchup of antiquity. The best comes from Gades' tuna works.

wool_cloth.name: Wool & cloth
wool_cloth.edictNote: mid-grade washed wool ~50 d.c./lb; Tarentine fine 175
wool_cloth.blurb: Tarentum and Laodicea-on-Lycus for fine cloth, Patavium for the mass market, Belgica and Britain for hooded winter cloaks.

linen.name: Linen
linen.edictNote: grades vary enormously in the Edict
linen.blurb: Egypt's second export after grain; Tarsus and Scythopolis compete.

papyrus.name: Papyrus
papyrus.edictNote: per kg equivalent; sold by the roll
papyrus.blurb: Every contract, ledger and letter in the empire is written on Nile marsh reed. A true Alexandrian monopoly.

iron.name: Iron & steel
iron.blurb: Every province smelts a little, but ferrum Noricum — steel from Noricum — and Spanish blades travel far.

copper.name: Copper & bronze
copper.blurb: Cyprus gave copper its name; Rio Tinto's slag heaps are visible from space.

tin.name: Tin
tin.blurb: No bronze without tin, and almost all of it streams from Cornwall through Isca. One thin supply line for a bronze-hungry empire.

silver.name: Silver
silver.blurb: Coinage metal: the Spanish mines paid for the legions for four centuries. The denarius is now barely half silver — inflation is coming.

gold.name: Gold
gold.blurb: Las Médulas in Spain (mountains washed away with water) and Dacia's Alburnus Maior feed the treasury.

marble.name: Marble & stone
marble.blurb: So heavy that only water can move it — which is why every great marble source is a harbour. Imperial porphyry comes from one mountain in the Egyptian desert.

timber.name: Timber
timber.blurb: Ships, roofs, scaffolds and fuel. Value-to-weight is so poor it rarely travels far — cedar of Lebanon and Alpine fir are the exceptions.

glass.name: Glass
glass.blurb: Blown glass is barely two centuries old and already everywhere; Phoenicia and Alexandria lead.

ceramics.name: Fine pottery
ceramics.edictNote: sold by the piece; ~ per kg
ceramics.blurb: Red-gloss sigillata: Arretium taught La Graufesenque, and now African Red Slip is conquering every table on the sea.

pepper.name: Pepper & spices
pepper.blurb: Monsoon cargo from Muziris: across the Indian Ocean to Berenice, by camel to Coptos, down the Nile to Alexandria. Pliny groused it drained 50M sesterces a year to India.

frankincense.name: Frankincense & myrrh
frankincense.blurb: Every temple, funeral and household shrine burns Arabian resin. The caravans pay Petra's tolls.

silk.name: Silk
silk.blurb: Worth its weight in gold, walked across Asia hand to hand — no Roman has ever seen China. Palmyra and the Red Sea are the two doors.

purple_dye.name: Purple dye
purple_dye.blurb: Ten thousand murex snails per toga stripe. Tyre's monopoly, Meninge's imitation, the emperor's colour.

amber.name: Amber
amber.blurb: Baltic gold, carried down the Amber Road to Carnuntum since Nero sent a knight to fetch it.

sources.label: Baetican oil estates
sources.note: The Guadalquivir valley: oil on an industrial scale, barged down to Hispalis.

sources.label: Tripolitanian oil
sources.note: Pre-desert olive farms with monumental presses; Severus showers his hometown in the proceeds.

sources.label: Istrian oil
sources.note: Premium oil for the Danube armies and north Italy.

sources.label: Campanian wine
sources.note: Falernian, Caecuban, Surrentine — the grand crus of Italy.

sources.label: Gallic bulk wine
sources.note: Mass-market wine in barrels — a Gallic invention — floods the western provinces.

sources.label: Layetanian wine
sources.note: Cheap, cheerful, and everywhere; Martial sneered at it.

sources.label: Chian premium
sources.note: The Bordeaux of antiquity.

sources.label: Gaditane garum works
sources.note: Tuna-based liquamen from the Atlantic weirs — the premium brand.

sources.label: Po valley wool
sources.note: Strabo: the carpets and cloaks of Patavium clothe Rome.

sources.label: Belgic cloaks
sources.note: The hooded caracallus — the emperor's nickname comes from wearing one.

sources.label: British birrus
sources.note: Waterproof wool cloaks, praised in the Edict itself.

sources.label: Scythopolitan linen
sources.note: Top-graded in the Price Edict.

sources.label: Nile delta papyrus marshes
sources.note: The only source in the world. When civil war cut the supply under Domitian, the empire panicked.

sources.label: Ferrum Noricum
sources.note: Naturally manganese-alloyed steel; the legions' preferred blades.

sources.label: Celtiberian steel
sources.note: Bilbilis blades quenched in the Salo — Martial's boast.

sources.label: Cypriot copper
sources.note: Aes Cyprium: the island that named the metal.

sources.label: Cornish tin streams
sources.note: Effectively the empire's only major source — every bronze workshop depends on this one supply line.

sources.label: Cartagena silver mines
sources.note: 40,000 slaves worked here in Polybius' day.

sources.label: Las Médulas gold
sources.note: Ruina montium: whole mountains washed away with aqueducts.

sources.label: Dacian gold (Alburnus Maior)
sources.note: The mines Trajan conquered Dacia to hold; miners' wax contracts survive.

sources.label: Proconnesian marble
sources.note: An island that is one quarry, right on the sea — the empire's cheapest good marble.

sources.label: Numidian giallo antico
sources.note: The golden-yellow stone of Simitthus, an imperial monopoly.

sources.label: Imperial porphyry
sources.note: One mountain in the eastern desert; the purple stone reserved for emperors.

sources.label: Mons Claudianus granite
sources.note: The Pantheon's porch columns came from this desert quarry.

sources.label: Cedar of Lebanon
sources.note: Hadrian fenced the best stands as an imperial forest.

sources.label: Phoenician glass
sources.note: Sidon's blowers claim the craft's invention.

sources.label: South Gaulish sigillata
sources.note: La Graufesenque: single kilns fire 30,000 vessels.

sources.label: African Red Slip
sources.note: Rides free as ballast on the grain ships — which is why it wins.

sources.label: Indian Ocean trade (via Berenice)
sources.note: The monsoon run: Muziris to Berenice, camel to Coptos, barge to Alexandria.

sources.label: Arabian incense caravans
sources.note: From Arabia Felix up the caravan road, tolled at Petra.

sources.label: Silk road via Palmyra
sources.note: Palmyrene caravans bring it from Parthian middlemen on the Euphrates.

sources.label: Tyrian purple works
sources.note: The double-dipped sacred purple; the shore reeks of murex.

sources.label: Meninx (Djerba) purple
sources.note: Africa's murex works — nearly as good, distinctly cheaper.

sources.label: Amber Road terminus
sources.note: Baltic amber, traded hand-to-hand across barbaricum to the Danube.

shocks.name: Nile flood fails
shocks.desc: A bad inundation: Egyptian surplus collapses and its grain price nearly doubles.

shocks.name: African drought
shocks.desc: Drought across the Maghreb: Africa's surplus halves.

shocks.name: Piracy returns
shocks.desc: The fleets have decayed; sea freight triples, as before Pompey swept the pirates.

shocks.name: Mare clausum (winter)
shocks.desc: November to March the open sea closes: no direct crossings, cautious coasting at a premium.

shocks.name: Plague (Antonine-style)
shocks.desc: Pestilence spreads along the very trade routes: all populations fall 15%.

shocks.name: War in the East
shocks.desc: War on the Euphrates: caravan luxuries spike, Mesopotamia's fields are ravaged.

edictSampler.price: 16 d.c. per castrensis modius of grain
